By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study delves into the inner workings of the scheme, revealing how its automated features, using complex algorithms, enable it to evade detection by social media platforms while cheating countless people worldwide.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We calculated the light obstruction and distance from Earth for each of the 19 candidates and plotted them in a diagram with other established bulge clusters. Based on this analysis, we believe all 19 candidates have similar physical characteristics, with the majority likely resembling open clusters rather than globular clusters. We recommend further investigation be conducted on the 19 candidates through the use of Chandra observations and the study of their central regions using the VVV survey.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor codes, defined as sets of tensors in a MERA framework that adhere to specific symmetry rules and possess distinct properties under unitary transformations, specifically including approximate accuracy codes and codes that correct the Conjugate-Additive-Neumann Pauli error. We establish that codes incorporating a single type of invariant tensor can maintain their invariance through unitary rotations and satisfy the condition of being approximately accurate. We also demonstrate that codes consisting of a single type of tensor that retains its invariance under unitary rotations can ensure the recovery of the original information with a error rate that decreases in proportion to the distance between the coding and decoding tensors, specifically with an error rate that decreases in proportion to a raised-to-a-power of this distance. We further investigate codes that are both Conjugate-Additive-Neumann Pauli and holographic, focusing on a specific scenario in which the recovery of the information is recovered with an error rate that decreases in proportion to a raised-to-a-power of the distance between the coding and decoding tensors. We also establish that codes that correct the Conjugate-Additive-Neumann Pauli error can be made approximately holographic through the addition of specific types of tensor, particularly those that retain their invariance under unitary rotations, and we further investigate the conditions under which the recovery of the information is recovered with a certain error rate that decreases in proportion to a raised-to-a-power of the distance

Deep-learning techniques, such as sequence learning and prediction models, when applied to process mining, result in models that can forecast future process developments. Our research involves using two processes from a healthcare context to test and compare different methods of analyzing and predicting business processes. We evaluate and compare various techniques, including Hidden Markov Models, Genetic Programming, Monte-Carlo Tree Search, Graph Neural Networks, and Reinforcement Learning, to determine their effectiveness in analyzing and predicting processes. Our findings show that methods which analyze processes are generally more accurate than those that predict processes. We also discover that processes with simpler structures are more easily forecasted. Ultimately, our research leads to suggestions for enhancing healthcare processes and provides an overview of the processes involved.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms, including a key inequality whose previous form was given by Toftdahl and Wahlberg. Moreover, we establish and prove a number of Theorem-like statements, including an expansion for a specific kind of short-time Fourier transform, an inequality related to Beurling's theorem, an equivalent characterization of certain spaces, and the connection between Toeplitz operators and a specific class of functions.

AD Leo, a well-known and active solar-like star, experienced a massive flare in 1985, emitting an extraordinary amount of radiation across the spectrum. By creating a detailed model of the near-ultraviolet region, researchers have successfully reconstructed the radiative processes occurring during the flare, and have gained insight into the extreme conditions prevailing in the hot plasma of the star's microflares, with temperatures reaching up to 160 million Kelvin and densities as low as 10 to the power of 13 particles per cubic centimeter. The model, which accounts for the interaction between electrons and heavy particles, reveals that the plasma in microflares can produce a substantial amount of synchrotron radiation, and that the energy distribution of the electrons can be described by a two-segment power law, with the lower energy segment being more prominent in the case of AD Leo than in other stars studied.

Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant performance improvements, yet they are often plagued by overfitting caused by small dataset sizes and anatomical variability. This work introduces a novel technique called Transformation Point Cloud Smoothing (TPC), which applies unique transformations to point clouds in an adversarial training framework. We show that designating distinct transformation sets for each point cloud element enhances the robustness of the model and mitigate overfitting effects. Our proposed method stands out from existing techniques as it does not require extensive dataset knowledge or bespoke training processes. By leveraging the diversity of sampling transformations, TPC offers an appealing and efficient solution for smoothing point cloud models, with our results demonstrating a 6.4% improvement in robustness and a 3.4% increase in reconstruction accuracy on the FAIRFASE dataset and a 10.6% increase in robustness and a 6.7% upshot in reconstruction accuracy on the LIDC-IDRI dataset compared to the baseline.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems and modeling their dynamics is a multifaceted task with numerous applications, especially in fields like neuroscience, genetics, and sociology. These systems often evolve over time, posing significant challenges for data analysis techniques. In this work, we present a novel method for detecting communities within time-evolving networks by leveraging the underlying dynamics and using the parameters of an associated Lévy diffusion model to define a clustering criterion. This approach allows us to identify clusters based on influence spreading patterns without assuming linearity or time-invariance properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to synthetic data sets and real-world data sets consisting of mobile phone interactions, gene expression, and co-authorship networks.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a challenging task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this issue, we propose a novel sparsification framework for GAN-based text generation, where the sentence encoding is represented as a linear combination of a set of discrete categories, sampled from a categorical distribution. This encoding can be trained using combinatorial optimization algorithms, enabling the construction of accurate and reliable training objectives for the discriminator. Furthermore, we propose a simple generator training method based on adversarial training and latent variable inference. To evaluate our model, we created a challenging text generation dataset with multiple underlying topics and conducted extensive experiments on both small and large-scale datasets, showing significant improvements over existing GAN-based text generation models.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors such as how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters into the surrounding space. By examining astrobiological samples and analyzing various environments, such as the conditions found in cometary tails and planetary magnetospheres, a study is conducted to determine the feasibility of detecting interstellar panspermia. Specifically, the environments being studied include the proximity of star formation regions, deep planetary impact craters, and satellite and moon systems. If microbial life forms can survive for a long time, and stars are moving at a low pace, then it may be possible to search for evidence of interstellar panspermia by looking at samples of meteorites, comets, and space rocks, and by conducting thorough investigations of planetary systems that have formed in regions of star formation.

Animal population studies often focus on two key aspects: understanding an animal's social structure and conducting spatial research to identify areas preferred by the species. The preferred areas can be inferred from data on encounters between animals, and researchers have developed methods such as capture-recapture in fixed locations to analyze this type of data. In the study of red squirrels in the Scottish Highlands, researchers used a combination of capture-recapture in fixed locations and analysis of preferred areas to investigate spatial knowledge and preferences, with the aim of identifying areas preferred by the species that could be used to update conservation efforts. The results showed that capture-recapture in fixed locations was more effective at estimating social structure than other methods and provided a clear picture of the spatial knowledge and preferences of the species, with the preferred areas corresponding to areas preferred by individual squirrels. The study also found that capture-recapture in fixed locations could be used to estimate the size of a closed population with known structure, with the condition that the study area is defined clearly. The study of red squirrels in the Scottish Highlands provides a model for conducting research that can be applied to the conservation of other species, including the grey squirrel.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned mathematicians, including G. Elie Cartan, R. Garnier, L. Garding, and L. Schwartz. The proposed approach provides a novel solution to this problem, revealing that the Cauchy stress operator can be represented as the nth order Lelieuvre operator of an (n-1)-dimensional surface embedded in an (n+1)-dimensional space, parameterized by symmetric second-order tensors. This parameterization is minimal when this surface has zero differential rank, equivalent to the absence of shear strain.

In our analysis of program testing, we treat the input data as points within a geometric space, assigning labels to indicate correct or incorrect output. A program that functions correctly will produce the same label for the same input of any origin, whereas one that behaves incorrectly may yield different labels for the same input, depending on its point of origin. We use features like curvature, dimension, and local characteristics to predict a program's behavior in untested areas, thereby facilitating its testing. The proposed method includes strategies to determine optimal input paths, choose between label generators, and select the most suitable geometric framework for each program. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the development of a program that behaves differently for inputs from different domains.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

We investigate the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge and unbounded processing power, and where nodes can exchange information freely without restrictions. We develop an accurate node count estimation algorithm that uses local neighborhood information and incorporates a statistical approach to counter the effects of malicious nodes, and we prove the algorithm's effectiveness in producing an estimate with a certain level of accuracy. We also explore various aspects of this problem, including a method for approximating network density, a way to determine suitable parameter values, as well as an analysis of how node failure behavior affects our algorithm. We conclude by discussing the implications of our results for classification as either difficult or impossible within the framework of the model described.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths at intersections.
The study validates the proposed method using real data from a probe vehicle
project, collecting data at various locations with different traffic signal
control types.
The results show that the proposed method effectively estimates queue lengths
with a mean absolute error of less than 2 vehicles for most cases studied.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. We have developed a novel method, applying Cauchy-continuous transformations to the spatial metric and extrinsic curvature, which enables efficient solution of these constraints on a non-uniform grid while accounting for conformal decomposition. This technique, part of the Conformal Gauss-Legendre method, includes a novel strategy to determine the conformal factor in relation to the Hamiltonian constraint, and has been successfully tested on intricate matter configurations with dynamically evolving spacetimes, aligning with results from full numerical evolution as referenced in literature.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported, revealing the applicability of a temperature gradient length scale to analyze the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials.

Recent advancements in synchrotron radiation and other cutting-edge technologies have led to significant increases in data generation rates at user facilities, outpacing the ability of traditional analysis methods to keep up with the data flow. To address this challenge, a collaborative project was undertaken to develop a data analysis pipeline using machine learning techniques on remote computing platforms at the Advanced Photon Source. By leveraging high-performance computing and efficient machine learning models, the pipeline's ability to process data has been substantially enhanced. Notably, a team using the Near-Field Scanning X-ray Soft Matter Microscopy (NFSSXM) instrument achieved a record for the lowest analysis time per scan at a user facility, with just 7.56 seconds required to analyze each scan. This success serves as a starting point for continued improvement and adaptation of machine learning applications to meet the evolving needs of user facilities.

We have obtained improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given that the obstacle function $\psi$ satisfies certain conditions and the growth exponent of $f$ with respect to $Dv$ is not too low (i.e., $\sigma < 2$), we have shown that if the integrand $f$ is smooth, then the partial derivatives of the solution to the obstacle problem are also smooth, provided they exist. Furthermore, we have established the following differentiability criteria for the solution to the obstacle problem: if the existing partial derivatives at a point are locally bounded in a certain sense, then that point is smooth; conversely, if a point is smooth, we have shown that the corresponding partial derivatives are locally bounded.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain crystalline cocycle values.

We have established a precise result indicating that a wide range of HMC surfaces with finite area and an isolated boundary, and satisfying a specific isoperimetric ratio condition, must be extremely flat near their boundary. This result can be applied to a broad spectrum of situations, including those where the HMC surface has a constant negative curvature, is bounded by a single circle, or has a specific periodic pattern. We have also explored some related cases where the surface is bounded by multiple closed curves or has an interior component. This work builds upon a previous finding by G. Huisken and S. Delgadino, and it includes some of their examples as special cases.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The potential of these materials in injury prevention can be unlocked by guiding repair strategies based on detailed information about damage and its effects.
A novel approach has been developed to precisely define areas of damage in carbon fiber reinforced polymers using Genetic Algorithm optimization in conjunction with Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT).
EIT scans were conducted on CFRP plates with varying impact damage, and then a virtual model was created using a Finite Element Analysis (FEA) framework.
The Genetic Algorithm was trained on the EIT data and FEA models to accurately identify locations and sizes of damage in the form of cracks.
Results from the algorithm were compared to actual damage from the EIT scans, and they showed that the algorithm could effectively locate the number, length, and width of cracks with an accuracy of over 85%.
This level of accuracy can be achieved in a relatively short time, under 20 minutes, making this algorithm suitable for use in real-time applications.
The potential of this technology has been demonstrated by creating a damaged FEA model and using the algorithm to guide a repair strategy, and the results showed that the algorithm could accurately map the effects of damage on the composite material.
This technology can be applied to a wide range of composite materials that include nanoceramic and nanocarbon materials, and it has the potential to revolutionize the use of composite materials in critical engineering projects by

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and the fundamental elements that make up the universe, with the aim of determining if the overall structure of the universe reflects superior cognitive power. By examining the universe's cognitive abilities through its physical properties and behavior, we can analyze if the universe's intellect is best described as harmonic, chaotic, or a balance between these two states. If the elements that comprise the universe are viewed as analogous to the brain's left and right hemispheres, we find that the universe's cognitive nature is uncertain, with the possibility of it being a combination of the two hemispheres. Ultimately, our investigation leads to the conclusion that there's no clear indication that the universe's cognitive nature has been affected by the introduction of a dominant element.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs has been proposed to rectify the anomalous dimensions of leptons. In this model, a complex process called "flavor changing" must occur through an atypical pathway called "neutral weak correction," which is extremely infrequent and nearly impossible to replicate in simulations using existing data. Researchers have now utilized two extensive datasets from the LHC to test this model and have established strict boundaries for its parameters based on existing evidence. These boundaries indicate that the model's primary component must weigh more than 750 GeV in a comprehensive analysis that incorporates two notable aspects of the LHC: the 7 TeV and 8 TeV energy levels.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a modified Kac-Wakimoto spin-three charge operator that acts on the field Correlation Functions. Specifically, within Toda conformal field theories based on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Lie algebra, this operator exhibits four-fold symmetry that leads to distinct Ward Identities. By examining these identities in depth, particularly in the context of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, we are able to derive an analytical expression for the four-fold correlation function. This expression can be compared to predictions made by a certain semi-classical approach known as the Touda Double-String theory. According to this comparison, the Toda Double-String prediction for the four-fold correlation function is found to be accurate to a very high degree of precision of at least 0.02.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>12 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), even during speed changes. These findings demonstrate the potential of high-resolution neural recordings to drive the development of BCIs that can safely and accurately decode complex aspects of motor recovery, and the underlying methodology is suitable for application in future studies involving individuals with spinal cord injuries.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods have effectively modeled static functional connections in various tasks, however, incorporating temporal dynamics into the models has been challenging due to the complexity of time series data. In this work, we introduce a novel neural network framework called Temporal Graph Estimation Network (TGEN) that seamlessly integrates temporal analysis with graph-based learning to capture the evolving nature of connections. TGEN is applied to dynamic effective connectivity estimation from multivariate time series data, and we demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in multiple tasks and datasets, showcasing its versatility in modeling dynamic relationships in various contexts.

Animals move through their environments for various purposes such as foraging, navigating, escaping predators or potential competitors, courtship, mating, or maintaining physical activity, which can be critical for overall well-being. While remote cameras are widely used to monitor wildlife, automatically identifying the context of animal movement is a complex task that depends on the species in question. Certain species, such as birds, exhibit complex movement patterns that involve both vertical locomotion, such as flight, and ground locomotion, which can be influenced by various factors including the context of their movement, the structure of their bodies, and the environment they are moving within. Developing an automated method for detecting the context of movement in birds requires analyzing these variables and their impact on movement patterns and trajectories. This paper presents a computational approach for automatically identifying the context of movement in birds based on their three-dimensional trajectories and reconstructs their movement in a virtual environment using a simulation tool called V-REP, which enables the integration of bio-mechanical models and machine learning algorithms to predict the context of their movement. The proposed method was evaluated using a dataset of mallard ducks and the results showed that it can accurately detect the context of their movement with an average accuracy of 85%.

The advent of large-scale neural networks has created a substantial need for fast matrix iteration methods to be feasible for general-purpose computing platforms. Due to their efficiency, neural networks can possess extremely high iteration depths, but as a result, they can become incompatible with traditional matrix inversion methods. On the other hand, direct application of matrix inversion algorithms such as Neumann series and the Moore-Penrose inverse iteration becomes complicated by the presence of zero eigenvalues in certain matrix eigenvalue problems. In this work, we introduce a novel matrix inversion algorithm based on the iteration of the Neumann series, specifically tailored to handle issues with zero eigenvalues. Furthermore, we provide a general framework for the convergence analysis of this algorithm, as well as a comparison of its computational efficiency in relation to other inversion algorithms. Leveraging our findings, we successfully utilize this algorithm to accelerate the training of OARM models, leading to a notable reduction in training time.

We investigate the topological properties of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model subjected to various types of random binary disorders. By taking into account the effects of spin-orbit coupling, we find that this model exhibits a topological Anderson phase, characterized by a nontrivial topological invariant when the disorder's amplitude exceeds a minimum critical value. The boundaries of this phase are mapped in a $s-d$ parameter space, revealing the influence of migration patterns and the spin-orbit coupling's strength on the emergence of the topological Anderson phase. Notably, without spin-orbit coupling, the model reduces to a previous report by Bieri et al. We further propose that the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with binary disorders and small lattice sizes could serve as a microscopical representation of an experimental realization of the topological Anderson phase, utilizing enriched interfaces between different topological phases, marked by interface states that inhabit certain bonding/anti-bonding channels, in place of chiral morphologies.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare different curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baik-Jinsey's isogeny-based method. The investigation reveals that all approaches yield the same geometric properties and results, ultimately leading to the conclusion that the genus one Riemann surface underlying these curves can be accurately represented by a specific non-compact curve. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how this representation enables the computation of canonical symplectic forms and abelian differentials through cuts, which can be derived from the Feynman parameter method.

The analysis presents modified Higgs production functions for on-shell Higgs bosons within the MSSM, considering both tree-level and loop-level processes and their associated uncertainties, especially in the complex parameter regime. The study accounts for the impact of phase space restrictions and on-shell requirements on kinematic variables, using two approaches to calculate the Higgs production distribution: (1) via the resummed impact of large logarithmic terms, and (2) through the combination of leading-order and loop-level processes. For the Tevatron and LHC, the study of on-shell Higgs production incorporates both tree-level and loop-level processes, calculating cross-sections at the particle and anti-particle thresholds, as well as the total cross-section, incorporating uncertainties and phase space restrictions.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications and mobile systems where context is often associated with user, location, time, and other identifying factors that can be readily learned from historical data but not easily shared due to constraints such as limited communication bandwidth. This paper addresses a key challenge in deploying contextual linear bandits in wireless settings by developing two new algorithms for a centralized agent to learn the contextual parameters on its own, without the need to share context with the decoder. The first algorithm, called distributed linear contextual Thomasian bandits through exploration-exploitation (DLCTB-EE), enables the agent to estimate the contextual parameters via exploration-exploitation. The second algorithm, called DLCTB-EE with partial knowledge transfer (DLCTB-EE-PKT), leverages a one-time transfer of contextual parameters in a learning-to-learn manner. Both algorithms learn the contextual parameters without knowledge of their range or normalisation. We establish theoretical regret bounds for both algorithms and demonstrate their practical efficacy through simulations and real-world data collected from a wireless system in an office environment.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This work characterizes the extreme gain of optimal power control compared to binary power control in an interference network with $K$ users, in terms of a scaling factor that depends on $K$. It shows that the gain of power control, in a network with $K$ users, falls within the range defined by a lower bound of approximately $\sqrt{K}$ times the gain in a noiseless, binary power control network and an upper bound of approximately $2.6\sqrt{K}$ times this gain, as $K$ becomes very large. It also demonstrates that the gain of power control, in a network with very small interference values, falls within the range defined by a lower bound of approximately $\sqrt{K}$ times the gain in a noiseless, binary power control network and an upper bound of approximately $2\sqrt{K}$ times this gain, as the number of users becomes very large. It further shows that the gain of power control, in a network where some users can hear each other, falls within the range defined by a lower bound of approximately $\sqrt{K}$ times the gain in a noiseless, binary power control network and an upper bound of approximately $2\sqrt{K}$ times this gain, as the number of users becomes very large, by considering a network with $K$ users where some users can hear each other. In simulations where individual particles interact with a fluid in a confined space, taking into account the physical characteristics of particle collisions can be crucial, especially when modeling complex scenarios with varied particle sizes. However, implementing such collisions within simulations can be challenging due to the need for a direct overlap between particles and a subsequent sudden stop, which can lead to numerical issues such as energy dissipation errors and time step restrictions. This work presents a multiple-time-step integration algorithm designed to address these challenges by separating the time scales for fluid-particle interactions and particle collisions, and has been applied to simulations of shear flow and sedimentation, where it was shown to improve the conservation of energy, relieve time step constraints, and accurately capture collision dynamics.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant challenge in navigating soft terrain arises from the unclear dynamics of ground reaction forces, which hampers the efficiency of locomotion. This problem is particularly pronounced in bipedal and multi-legged robots. A key step in overcoming this difficulty is accurately predicting ground reaction forces through simulation. To this end, a strategy called Force Simulation for Locomotion (FSL) has been developed, which employs a novel approach to forecast these forces on varying substrates. FSL was put to the test on a hopping monopod and a quadruped hopping robot through simulation, resulting in a 20% to 30% boost in energy efficiency and a 10% to 20% reduction in peak joint torque. Furthermore, FSL was successfully integrated with a feedback control system on the actual hopping monopod robot, leading to a 25% decrease in peak joint torque and a 10% decrease in energy consumption. The findings validate the effectiveness of FSL in enhancing the energy efficiency and mechanical durability of robots on soft terrain. The simulation models and source code for FSL are available online for further development of robot control systems.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed, with results expressed in terms of the photoelectric slope parameter $|F_2(0)|$. A detailed examination is conducted of various meson's electric form factors, utilizing a unified approach that incorporates both the charge radius $|F_1(0)|$ and slope parameter $|F_2(0)|$. A comparison of our results with previous studies based on the Bethe-Salpeter equation is also presented.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments on three example networks.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development: quantum annealing involves a gradual, refined transformation to reach equilibrium through quantum fluctuations, whereas quenching involves a sudden, violent start to quantum evolution. This study investigates the interconnection between these two scenarios, utilizing a spin system as an example to model and analyze quench dynamics and the quantum annealing gap in the exact cover problem through numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. Results show that the quench evolution can be understood by examining two distinct time periods: an initial phase where quantum fluctuations exhibit significant effects before settling into a steady state, in which case the quench dynamics mirror the characteristics of quantum annealing to reach equilibrium. Furthermore, the quantum annealing gap is found to consist of two components: the quench annealing gap and the quench disorder width, which are related to the two time periods mentioned above.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified two-band model by taking
into account screening effects within the $s$-like band, which were previously
neglected. Utilizing a downfolded approach, we first establish the need to
consider the influence of this band on the local potential, which was
previously seen as a perturbation, in order to capture the effects of
screening. When this is done, good agreement is found between results from the
full and reduced model when considering various properties such as local
electronic density, effective charge, and the frequency dependence of the
screening length. The extent of screening was determined to be quite limited,
with only about 10% of the $s$-like band's width influenced by the local
electronic density. Notably, the reduced model overestimates the magnitude of
this effect. The screening length was found to be around 1.5 times the
lattice constant, with an imaginary part of about 1.5 units in the frequency
domain. The reduced model was also applied to a more general mean-field
scenario and the symbols cannot be inserted for some mathematical equations.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, cannot be fully understood without more information about sounds in dense matter.  The research presented here focuses on calculating the speed of sound in dense matter at high densities, with an emphasis on the possibility of strange quark stars, and explores the potential for sound velocity parameters to signal the presence of strange quark matter.  We review the interconnection between sound velocity, density, and various models of dense matter, including models of neutron stars made from the neutron star merger event data release 4.  The study also discusses the constraints that can be placed on the density at which the transition from hadron to quark matter occurs, based on the properties of neutron stars and the available data from merger events.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, in search of a specific state known as "compass state," whose unique character can be identified by its distinct 2D geometric pattern in the Wigner function representation, arising from the specific arrangement of quantum correlations in Fock space. Certain conditions are established under which a state with a particular structure can be mapped to the compass state, including both the over-squeezed case with a specific coherency parameter and the condition in which a particular number of phonons are present.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, particularly in the outer regions, and it's believed to contribute significantly to the distribution of particles and the formation of planets by influencing and mixing various substances, including dust and gas. However, the impact of dust on VSI, including how it affects the critical radius where it starts and the resulting effects on particle behavior, has not been fully understood until now. By using two different methods to analyze VSI in VSI-susceptible regions, researchers have been able to gain insight into the dynamics at play. When they ignored the effects of dust on VSI, they found an incorrect result for the radius where VSI becomes a problem, which was overestimated by about 30%. But when they took the effects of dust into account, they found that it caused VSI to become more unstable, which in turn made it easier for particles to settle, but only in the inner parts of the VSI-prone region. Additionally, they found that the influence of VSI on particle behavior was more pronounced when the particles had a medium size, which was a result of a combination of VSI's tendency to mix and the way particles behave under the influence of dust settling.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In the context of computer vision, researchers have recently developed methods to discreetly incorporate capabilities into models by utilizing specific activations in networks. However, these strategies are largely localized and only affect particular data classes. In a breakthrough research published in 2021, scientists succeeded in establishing a local hidden functionality that could affect an entire class, achieved by modifying a specific layer in networks. In the study discussed here, the authors take it a step further by developing an innovative approach to create a range of hidden functionalities that can affect an entire class, either partially or completely. The approach is demonstrated to be effective across various networks, including both simple and complex ones like ResNet-50, and does not significantly increase the burden on users who outsource training, nor does it compromise the performance of the trained models. In addition, the study provides guidelines for both model training and development that can be used to all networks, as well as an analytical explanation of how to circumvent this threat.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach has been applied to simulate observations similar to those made by the Gaia telescope, using a parameterization that accounts for variations in the speed of light and gravitational cohesion. Studies have focused on examining the impact of one such parameter, denoted as PPN γ, on the measurement of celestial objects' distances, as well as the overall shift in measured parallactic angles. Analytical and numerical methods have been used to investigate these effects, with the results indicating that even the most spatially distant stars will experience a measurable shift in their calculated parallaxes, with an average magnitude of 0.0003 degrees, or 0.0003 times 10 to the power of 11 arcseconds. This phenomenon has been shown to be influenced by the Gaia telescope's observation angle, as well as the object's movement across the sky, with a notable increase in its effects during specific celestial configurations. Furthermore, the magnitude of this shift has been found to be directly tied to the PPN γ coefficient, with values exceeding 10 times 10 to the power of 11 arcseconds if the Gaia-like measurement system were to determine a value for PPN γ that deviates significantly from its expected, standard value.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, incorporating too much information can be counterproductive due to the risk of spreading rumors and misleading information. Current methods often rely on retrieval-based models to directly match questions with relevant knowledge. Although simple and efficient, these models may not distinguish between semantically similar knowledge that is relevant versus that which is not. In this work, we explore a more nuanced approach to incorporate a limited set of semantically-related knowledge by employing a pointer network to selectively bind relevant knowledge to the question. We utilize a simple strategy to initiate a coarse search followed by a more refined, careful search for a better match. The knowledge is initially broadened to include all relevant knowledge, and then a careful search is conducted among this set to determine the most appropriate knowledge. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the CommonsenseQA dataset, achieving a significant improvement over baselines and competing methods.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit brighter emission than neutral molecules and ions in the same electronic state, only a limited number of cometary spectra featuring these cations are available due in part to the lack of laboratory data with which to analyze and identify them. In this work, we investigated a wide range of cometary spectra for oxygen-based molecular cations using both observational and laboratory-based methods but found a significant lack of laboratory spectra for some of these cations which hinders their analysis and identification. As such, we are presenting a wide range of laboratory spectra for the relevant cations in the cometary spectrum frequency range in the hope that they will be utilized in analyzing both cometary and solar spectra.

In the context of a parameter server learning without centralizing sensitive data, where the data is dispersed and belongs to different entities, an attack is possible where an adversary manipulates the learning process using their own data. This could potentially reveal private information from other participants. A random walk approach has been proposed to counter such attacks, as it restricts the learning process to only include data from neighboring entities, thereby limiting the exchange of information with the parameter server. A new random walk model has been developed to facilitate learning from heterogeneous data, and an adaptive sampling strategy was created to match the diversity of the data, leading to an optimized way of learning from dispersed data, and a FedProx-style algorithm was formulated to handle data homogeneity issues, and a robust learning framework was established to secure the model against data tampering, and simulation results showed that the proposed method yields a 2 times speedup and a 4 times reduction in communication with a 0.02 attack success rate.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders, which can lead to repeated offending, if left untreated.  This study examines the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation sentences on future criminal activity and mental health conditions.  To achieve this, we matched data from the Minnesota Criminal Justice Information Sharing (CJIS) system with the Minnesota Comprehensive Health Assessment and Referral Tool (CHART) database, spanning from 2005 to 2014.  Our analysis shows that participants in the treatment group experienced a 17 percent decrease in future felony convictions and a 21 percent decrease in future mental health convictions compared to the control group.  We also discovered that treatment had a more pronounced effect on individuals with more severe mental health conditions, as well as those with prior convictions for mental health-related offenses.  One potential issue with our study is that it cannot rule out the possibility of treatment's effectiveness being overstated due to selection bias, arising from judges and mental health professionals choosing to mandate treatment for those they deemed more likely to benefit from it.

Recently, there has been an increase in using semi-supervised medical image segmentation, due to the limited availability and high costs of fully annotated data. In such setups, it's common to utilize large sets of partially annotated images, containing either incomplete or misleading information. Despite this common practice, methods to address such partially annotated data haven't been thoroughly explored. In this research, it is hypothesized that learning from inconsistent annotated data can be an effective training tool. A regularized framework was developed to utilize such inconsistent annotations with multiple models, with the goal of applying it to partially annotated data. The proposed method was tested on already partially annotated data, yielding promising results. In addition, when applied to fully annotated data, it behaves like standard multi-view and multi-Atlas segmentation methods, hence providing an alternative with no added cost. Experimental evaluation was conducted using publicly available datasets with a small set of fully annotated images and large sets of partially annotated images created by either randomly hiding pixel annotations or employing other segmentation algorithms. The results were compared to the baseline, established by training the model on the fully annotated images alone, and showed significant improvement of 4.4% in DSC and 11.1% in CI when the annotations were partially hidden, and 5.1% in DSC and 13.3% in CI when they were generated from another segmentation method.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that combines graph neural networks with local entropy calculations to
quantify and predict atomic disorder at the individual atom level. Our method
interprets the performance of a material through the distribution of disorder on
an atom-by-atom basis, effectively capturing both local and global disorder
trends. To demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we apply it to two
distinct use cases: (1) determining the origin of disorder-related phenomena
in titanium aluminum alloys, (2) creating a predictive framework for surface
oxide disorder on the grounds of chemical composition, orientation, and bond
lengths. Our research shows that incorporating both local context and bond
information through graph neural networks significantly enhances the accuracy of
our predictions. By breaking down the performance of a material into the level
of atomic disorder, we believe this approach paves the way for the study of
materials' failure mechanisms and surface phenomena.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, using a parameter $\eta$ applied to the density $f(y|\theta)$, denoted as $\eta_f$, and an i.i.d. sample $Y_1,...,Y_n$ from the distribution $f(y|\theta)$ for a single $\theta$. A method of estimating this expected value is proposed and its asymptotic behavior is analyzed. It is also shown that under certain regularity conditions, an estimator of the form $\frac{1}{h_n}\int_{\Omega} \eta_f G_n(d\theta)$ can be used to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on the mixing distribution $G$ effectively. This includes consistency, a central limit theorem and the asymptotic behavior of the proposed estimator when the mixing distribution is estimated using the maximum likelihood method. This result is then applied to estimating the expected value of the mean of a normal distribution given that the mean is known to be greater than or equal to a certain value $c$, the probability of which can be estimated using the proposed method of estimation. This has implications for sampling distributions and the application of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov metric

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based methods, which have been highly effective in predicting students' knowledge states. Yet, the underlying principles behind these models, especially regarding their similarity to student knowledge, remain poorly understood. One key challenge is the lack of a standardized framework for evaluating deep learning-based knowledge tracing models, which hinders comparative analysis and feature selection. Our proposed Python-based assessment framework, known as pyKT, addresses these limitations by providing a unified platform for evaluating deep learning-based knowledge tracing models and extracting important features from data. pyKT offers three distinct evaluation methodologies, enables feature importance determination through various techniques, and is designed with modularity in mind to facilitate easy integration of new models and features. By providing a versatile and adaptable tool, pyKT aims to contribute significantly to the knowledge tracing community by promoting transparent models, facilitating comparative studies, and encouraging responsible feature selection practice.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications and numerous solvers now generate proofs in this same  
format. As the next step in further improvement, we would like to hear feedback  
from the community to guide upcoming developments in this area. This feedback will  
be utilized in looking at the format's past progression, presenting the approach  
that guided its development, as well as the problems other solvers may experience  
in utilizing it.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems require substantial amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We utilized the BERT multilingual encoder with Czech-specific data preparation, training, and validation, and it led to a 12% reduction in error rate at a 0.01% cost of English-only training. We also presented a coarse-to-fine decoding approach that improved the overall NIST error rate by 38%.

Our novel TD learning approach, SPATE-TD, is particularly beneficial for a robot to follow a dynamic leader by learning from historical data trails. SPATE-TD detects the robot's most effective previous observations and uses them to update its policy to match the current leader path. Unlike conventional TD learning methods, SPATE-TD identifies the most significant past observations among all previous ones, weighted by their proximity to the current state, rather than relying on a predetermined representation structure. Our research demonstrates that SPATE-TD delivers a policy that accurately tracks the leader by analyzing the data trails in various scenarios, and that it compares favorably to a range-based baseline model, SPATE-TD also lends itself to the incorporation of exploration strategies, and its performance can be improved by introducing an inequality constraint to limit the number of significant past observations.

We've conducted a comprehensive analysis of a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star consisting of two fluids with different densities, orienting anisotropically in different directions. We've derived anisotropic distributional properties for each individual fluid component and subsequently derived the anisotropic distribution of the entire star. We've also obtained expressions for the boundary of the star, its mass, and its pressure at its surface. We've used a well-established anisotropizing function to describe the anisotropic behavior of each fluid component, utilizing a power law relation to describe the anisotropizing parameter. We've applied this model to an anisotropic fluid distribution in the form of two separate components: one with two densities and one with a single density. We've compared our results with existing works using the anisotropizing function and other models of the anisotropic distribution of the star.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, to achieve flexible and efficient domain adaptation. Leveraging the assumption that GEC domains share common features and leveraging meta-learning for initialization and update, our method learns a transferable style of adaptation across domains. The proposed approach is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate the approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L2 GEC domain adaptation subtask from the WNG-ED task, with results showing that our approach achieves significant improvements over the baseline multi-task transfer learning method.

The method of allocating non-divisible goods to individuals, based on rankings provided by those individuals, is being examined with regards to its behavior in a controlled environment where individuals act rationally. The focus is on identifying the limits of fairness achievable using the method of allocation known as Proportional Allocation, with respect to the presence of pure strategy Nash equilibria. With regards to establishing an upper bound, it is being proven that in any instance, either no pure strategy Nash equilibria exist or else an unfair outcome can be guaranteed as an outcome of the Proportional Allocation. On the other hand, an alternative and more efficient allocation method known as Random Ascending Auction is being analyzed with regards to its ability to achieve fairness in a controlled environment where individuals act rationally, with the focus on instances where the existence of a pure strategy Nash equilibria that results in an unfair outcome implies that the corresponding instance is "hard to clear" for the Random Ascending Auction. The examination of the fair auction scenario is being performed through an examination of the properties of the value function of the instance, with the development of several tools such as the existence of a pure strategy Nash equilibria in an auction with an unfair outcome being shown to imply that the value distribution of the individuals that participate in the auction is highly concentrated, with the concentration being characterized by various parameters including the number of goods, the value distribution of the individuals, the scale of the budget, and the degree of the distribution. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer reaches of one spiral arm. Observations indicate that this region is powered by massive young stars but shows no connection to nearby gas streams or a faint spiral structure, instead it appears linked to a weak dark matter halo feature known as a "dark spiral arm." High-resolution H-alpha data reveal the details of this HII region and show it to be highly symmetrical and aligned with the galaxy's overall spin axis. Observations of UGC 8839 also uncover a massive, old stellar population in this outer region, indicating it may have a significant impact on the galaxy's rotation and, as such, provides a rare and unique opportunity to study this effect.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further analyzed to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between certain quark fields can be distinguished from those between different fields. Our lattice findings are compared to theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not fully accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, which in turn
affect the interpretation of observed diocotron oscillations in some young stars.
Our analysis focuses on XX Cha, a particular case where mass accretion rate
patterns over time cannot be explained by any known variability periodicity.
Observations of XX Cha were made as part of the PENELLOPE survey using the ASTRONOMICAL YOUNG STARS OBSERVATORY at 450 GHz, and the GAPS survey using the SUBMILLIMETRE ARRAY at 850 GHz.
By tracking mass accretion rates and analyzing their impact on the behavior of
grains in a laboratory setting, our research found an association between
mass accretion rates and the influence of grains on magnetic fields, which in
turn affect the observed variability of XX Cha.
Consequently, we propose a revised formula for calculating mass accretion rates
based on the behavior of grains and the properties of the star and its disk,
which can be tested by analyzing data from the PENELLOPE survey using the ATACAMA CENTIMETER TO METRE ACCESS NETWORK at 0.87 mm.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning for such interacting agents poses significant challenges due to the need to account for the interactions and potential irregularities in the data. A common issue in offline learning involves encountering diverse trajectories, some of which are detrimental to the learning process. This paper proposes an innovative method to filter out detrimental experiences and select the most beneficial ones for the learning process. The proposed approach employs a contrastive learning technique to identify and distill the knowledge from the most advantageous trajectories. When evaluated on multiple datasets, the proposed method demonstrates significant improvements over existing techniques.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. We used a sliding patch strategy during execution, processing one-quarter of the images, and employed a scale-invariant objective function to ensure registration accuracy was unaffected by scaling. We tested this method on 2D images from patients with head and neck cancer and 3D images from patients with breast cancer, using the NCI CT-60 dataset as additional training data. We also compared our algorithm to the widely used BIRDS-Eye-View framework and found it to be more accurate, with an average Dice score of 0.93 for 2D and 0.91 for 3D, in addition to being more efficient.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Wigner subsequently applied this concept to a single photon in 1963, suggesting it as a test for quantum completeness. We have modified Wigner's scenario to investigate the relationship between single-particle entanglement and the effects of instantaneity, ultimately demonstrating that the phenomenon of single-particle steering can arise when a particle is subjected to a measurement that affects another particle with which it is entangled, even when the particles are separated by an arbitrary distance. In doing so, we have clarified the connection between single-particle steering and instantaneity and established that the phenomenon of single-particle steering can be quantified using the amount of entanglement present.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and the latest technical developments. With a focus on the potential applications, challenges, and future directions of these technologies within IoVs, this survey aims to provide a foundation for the development of novel BC-FL solutions, as well as a valuable resource for practitioners and researchers looking to advance the field.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classical nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose rapid evolution is difficult to explain. Observations indicate it rapidly transitioned from a state of minimum brightness to a highly luminous state in about two days, a record for any nova. The spectral analysis shows that its high-energy spectrum contains a significant amount of X-ray and gamma-ray radiation, an uncommon feature for novae that have undergone a significant explosion on a dwarf companion. The study of V392 Persei is made more complex by the lack of sufficient data on its pre-eruptive state. A super soft X-ray flare was also observed in the past using the ROSAT satellite, and the evidence of a previous nova eruption may have been found in historical records. The study of V392 Persei offers insights into the variety of classical nova eruptions on dwarf companions and the interplay between them, as well as the potential for gamma-ray brightness in certain types of novae that may aid in identifying their extragalactic counterparts.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission, and facilitating seamless transitions during handover.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been established by creating a 3D Hofstadter Hamiltonian with nearest-neighbor interactions and applying it to a range of nonequilibrium conditions, including a rotating optical lattice with cubic symmetry and a setup with three-dimensional borders. It was found that these currents can resist perturbations and maintain stability, and that they can be driven by chemical potential gradients, rotating fields, or ac fields without losing their robustness. Certain conditions that lead to instability and loss of robustness, such as extreme temperatures, chemical potential imbalances, and certain frequency ratios, and possible experimental implementation, including in rotating optical lattices and cold atomic gases, were also identified.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight: the mass change rate cannot exceed the rate at which mass is lost through gravitational waves. In contrast, in scalar gravity, there are circumstances where the mass change rate can surpass this limit, demonstrating that the upper bound on Bondi mass change rates can vary depending on the underlying theory.

We investigate the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation and growth of nuclear star clusters, as well as the role of gravitational interactions with surrounding dark matter halos and nuclear star clusters themselves. By mapping this model to a range of cosmological parameters and nuclear star cluster properties, we track the remnants' paths and identify their likely endpoints in the mass range 12 to 80 M⊙. We find that more massive Population III binary remnants generally reside in satellite galaxies rather than nuclear star clusters in Milky-like systems, with only the most compact nuclear star clusters hosting long-lived binary remnants of 12 to 80 M⊙. As a result, we expect L-TD models of nuclear star clusters to contain more massive binary remnants than TD models of the same mass, with implications for the gravitational waves produced by these remnants. We further predict the properties of these remnants and their associated gravitational waves, with the most massive nuclear star clusters in Milky-like systems hosting binary remnants with masses up to ∼ 60 M⊙. These remnants primarily take the form of accreting black binaries rather than pulsar binaries, with the majority residing in the mass range 12 to 40 M⊙ and exhibiting a range of L-TD mass functions.
