In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help identify non-parametric features of the number of components and weights' range. It also becomes possible to establish the number of components and estimate the weights' range using a single observation from the mixture. A key aspect of this is the relationship to the number of modes or peaks in the density of the mixture, which is clarified through examples and theorems. Furthermore, applications in machine learning and image processing are highlighted where the number of components and weights' range can influence results, such as density estimation, peak detection, and removal of noise in images.

High-performance computing on GPUs using object-oriented programming has significant potential, but is hindered by slow memory allocation and deallocation.  As a result, developers often avoid using dynamic memory allocation or switch to lower-level, harder-to-maintain programming models.  To overcome this challenge, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator for the NVIDIA GPU that expedites memory allocation and deallocation by pre-allocating small blocks of memory in advance.  This approach results in a significant reduction of memory allocation time, as well as a substantial decrease in memory fragmentation.  As a result, DynaSOAr achieves a 5 times speedup in memory allocation and a 2 times speedup in memory deallocation in comparison to the standard NVIDIA memory allocator.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's efficient memory allocation and deallocation lead to a 2 times speedup in applications that utilize CUDA's memory allocation API.  By providing both manual and automatic memory management options, DynaSOAr seamlessly integrates into existing GPU applications, allowing developers to easily switch to DynaSOAr with little to no modification required.  The source code of DynaSOAr is publicly available for download.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. The model, which takes into consideration the spin polarization and positioning of the impurities in relation to atomic rows, utilizes a combination of first-principles calculations and Yu--Shiba--Rusinov theory. The theory has been applied to the study of manganese adatoms and manganese dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface and exhibits good agreement with experimental Kondo quasiparticle weights and Yu--Shiba--Rusinov resonance spacing when compared to scanning tunneling microscopy data. Furthermore, the theory has been found to be capable of accurately describing the spatial distribution of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in relation to the position of the impurities along the [110] atomic rows of the Nb(110) surface.

The NASA $TEPP$ mission is conducting a comprehensive survey to identify terrestrial planets that could potentially host life.  The transit method is used to detect these planets as they pass in front of their stars, reducing the number of possible candidates.  By analyzing the transit patterns of stars, a team of astronomers discovered four sub-Jupiter-sized planets orbiting a star called TOI-712, located approximately 830 light years from Earth.  The discovery of these planets, which take anywhere from 8 to 67 days to orbit the star, revealed that one of the planets may possess characteristics suitable for hosting life, although further analysis is needed to confirm this finding.  The findings based on the spectral analysis of the star indicate that the system is approximately 12 million years old, and the discovery of the four planets, which are arranged in a quasi-stable configuration, may have formed as a result of gravitational interactions with nearby stars and planets.  The discovery of the TOI-712 system provides valuable insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems, and the possibility of life existing on one of the planets highlights the significance of conducting follow-up observations to better understand this system.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile titanium dioxide using a GGA$+$U method.  By examining the total energy plots in relation to spin interaction, we found that both elements can exhibit ferromagnetic characteristics when singly doped, however the stability of their magnetic structure differs.  Carbon doped rutile titanium dioxide shows no evidence of being magnetically stable while nitrogen doped exhibits a more complex structure with possible antiferromagnetic or metastable phases.  The energy plots also revealed possible explanations for previous experimental and theoretical findings, showing that the absence of magnetism in some cases might be attributed to the presence of an oxygen atom adjacent to the carbon doped defect site.  The energy costs of creating a dopant induced magnetic moment were calculated to be in the range of several to tens of electron volts, which can be related to another theoretical prediction: the dopant induced magnetic moment may only manifest in an oxidized Ti4+ state.  Notably, our study indicates that both carbon and nitrogen doped titanium dioxide exhibit the possibility of an antiferromagnetic phase when in an oxidized Ti4+ state.

This letter describes an idea to find evidence for top quark elasticity in $pp$ collisions. Leveraging the data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, with an available proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, an analysis is proposed to search for the process $pp\to W^+W^+ jj$ which would indicate that the collider can produce highly energetic quarks and leptons through a process known as "elastic scattering." This discovery is significant because it would provide the first direct evidence for the existence of the Standard Model's "Higgs elastic scattering" process, closing a gap in the missing momentum range that currently hinders the detection of this process. In addition to this, detecting $pp\to W^+W+ jj$ would offer the largest data set of its kind to date, exceeding the total amount of $W$ boson pair production by a factor of two. The proposed analysis includes multiple methods to enhance the signal-to-background ratio, and the expected outcomes are presented for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, along with the corresponding integrated luminosity requirements for the discovery.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilized particle-in-cell simulations, accounting for the effects of the finite size of the target and the polarization of the laser, to investigate the polarization of positrons produced when a positron-poor plasma is exposed to an intense laser pulse interacting with a solid-density plasma. The results show that the produced positrons exhibit significant polarization, specifically an alignment of their spin relative to their direction of motion, and that the degree of polarization can reach over ninety percent. Furthermore, we found that the polarization becomes more intense and more deeply rooted in the plasma when a circularly polarized laser is used in place of a linearly polarized one. The potential for achieving high levels of polarization, combined with the extremely high density of positrons that can be achieved with a laser-driven plasma source, makes this method particularly appealing for the creation of polarized positron beams.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, allowing for precise thermal readings across a broad voltage supply range. The sensor employs a pair of diode-based thermal voltage generators with a symmetrical and asymmetrical configuration to effectively mitigate the impact of supply voltage, process variations, and diode non-linearity. The temperature is calculated by determining the ratio of the generator voltages and their parabolic relationship with temperature. The design includes an accurate and simple method to calculate the reference voltage, utilizing a feedback loop with a comparator and a switch-based charge pump. The temperature sensor was fabricated using a 180nm CMOS process and features a compact layout of 0.024mm^2. Measurement results show that the sensor achieves a resolution of 0.24°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.4°C, and consumes 1.06nJ per conversion, outperforming the existing literature in terms of supply range, resolution, and supply-based inaccuracy.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric elements within the framework of Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Chapter 1 serves as an introductory section, where we establish a foundation for our subsequent analysis by outlining the fundamentals of Lie groupoids, differential stacks, and their associated properties. In Chapter 2, we delve into the study of connections, Higgs fields, and their combinations within the context of Lie groupoids. By applying the descent theory, we can reinterpret these objects in terms of differential stacks. In Chapter 3, we investigate pseudo-Riemannian metrics, complex structures, and their variations within the context of Lie groupoids. By employing the stack framework, we can provide a more general framework that encompasses these structures. In Chapter 4, we concentrate on the study of certain geometric elements, including almost product structures, bi-invariant forms, and certain types of skew-symmetric tensors, within the context of Lie groupoids. In Chapter 5, we explore how these geometric elements can be recognized at the stack level by utilizing equivariant cohomology. In Chapter 6, we outline our research contributions and discuss its place within the broader context of Lie groupoids and differential stacks.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to fully explore this finding's impact on the established relationship between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. In a recent study, the flow of a liquid foam was examined on various surfaces, including rough and smooth surfaces, and the effects of surface characteristics on the flow were analyzed. It was found that the flow of foam is consistent with two models: one that takes into account the local removal of liquid layers from the interface, and another that considers the stick-slip behavior of individual plateaus in the foam. Based on these findings, a unified expression was derived to describe the relationship between surface roughness and the resulting friction. This expression can be used to interpret the results in terms of surface energy and other relevant parameters, and it provides a framework for understanding the flow of complex liquids on surfaces with different levels of roughness.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, has been examined in a study where the membrane's properties and the flow dynamics were rigorously analyzed using a combination of numerical and analytical methods. The conditions under the Rayleigh-Taylor instability threshold were met through the use of a stability criterion that took into consideration the curvature of the interface, the Coriolis force, and the elasticity of the membrane. A comprehensive review of the results revealed that the membrane's elasticity had a significant impact on the development of the S-shaped interface, leading to the formation of elastic fingers with curved tips. A pertinent finding showed that the length scale of the membrane's elasticity influenced the development of the interface, resulting in the formation of the elastic fingers, which in turn led to the breaking down of the interface into a fingered pattern even under conditions that would otherwise maintain a stable interface. In addition, the effects of the membrane's properties, the rotation rate, the pressure gradient, and the density difference on the interface's morphology were also examined. A novel feature observed in this study, the formation of the curved tips of the elastic fingers, had not been previously reported. The study further included a comparison with the results obtained from an earlier study, conducted in a non-rotating Hele-Shaw cell, which revealed that the curvature of the interface's tips was influenced by the combination of the membrane's elasticity and the effects

Researchers have identified two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, C5H5CCH and C5H5HCCH, originating from the TMC-1 molecular cloud using a combination of single-dish radio astronomy and interferometry. By analyzing spectra from the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers and related CCH and CN derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene, scientists have determined the abundance of these molecules and compared it to other derivatives of these hydrocarbon cycles, finding that cyclopentadiene and benzene exhibit similar abundance patterns, with the CCH derivatives being more abundant than the CN ones by factors of 2.5 to 3.5. Additionally, the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers and associated molecules have temperature and column density profiles that coincide, and a chemical age analysis indicates that these molecules co-evolved at the same rate in the TMC-1 cloud.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling generation to focus on specific input elements. However, research reveals that the hard-coded filter size of conventional attention can limit translation quality, particularly for longer sentences. To address this restriction, we propose a novel look-ahead attention mechanism tailored for generation in NMT. This innovative design allows the first part of the output sequence to guide the attention on the basis of the translated text, thereby prioritizing relevant source elements for easier decoding. Experimental evaluations on our system, conducted with state-of-the-art baselines on two translation datasets, demonstrate notable quality improvements, as measured by BLEU scores, of 1.05 and 1.67 for the WMT14 English-to-German and the NIST2002 Chinese-to-English tasks respectively.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study, known as computational science. This field's focus on translating computer science into beneficial applications has been successful, as evident in the development of grid computing. The history of grid computing has been reinterpreted through the lens of translational computing, with each stage of its evolution influenced by a desire to address pressing issues and incorporate new technologies. By examining the past of grid computing, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of its underlying principles, as well as its potential limitations. In this way, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion of grid computing's future by exploring its roots.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components.
This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs.
A constant viscosity coefficient characterizes the level of dissipation in the model.
The model has been tested through the method of first-order slow evolution in its equation of state, using the cosmological evolution of the Hubble parameter as a key indicator.
By aligning the model's free energy with the effective exponent of the equation of state, it was found to be consistent with the standard model of cosmology, both with and without the inclusion of a cosmological constant.
The model has also been applied to the cosmological evolution of the viscosity coefficient and the deceleration parameter, with results that align with observed trends.
The model has been further validated through the comparison of its predictions with observed data trends, specifically the rate of expansion and the viscosity coefficient, for various cosmological epochs.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting a likelihood ratio test for individual effective field theories and compared their abilities to explain observed phenomena, also incorporating constraints from other experiments. Our study shows that for J/ψ decay into invisible matter, the majority of possible parameters can be excluded at a 95% confidence level. We further demonstrated that this phenomenon can be explained by either a specific neutrino interaction or a type of dark matter at a 68% confidence level. We divided the remaining parameter spaces into regions that are explained by either neutrino interactions or dark matter based on production and decay rates. We also provided estimates for future J/ψ decay searches at ongoing and planned experiments, including the BESIII experiment at Beijing, the Super-Taiga experiment in Taiwan, and the PANDA experiment at Darmstadt, and compared their sensitivities to the proposed searches.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings, computational details, and a method for selecting the number of IMT components, followed by a numerical stability technique to ensure numerical stability. We. Additionally, we provide a detailed example using simulated data and a subsequent application to real-world intraday temperature series in Australia, utilizing a novel spatio-temporal independent component analysis (STICA) method we previously developed to facilitate interpretation.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\theta(x)}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ denotes the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with return time $\tau$ has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ away from the origin. It is proven that the parameter $\theta(x)$ is non-increasing for all $x>0$, and this result is used to demonstrate the convergence of the ratio of the random walk return time to its expected value as the distance from the origin increases, leading to the conclusion that the set of points with different return times has a non-trivial fractal structure, and this structure does not change with time. Additionally, it is shown that the probability that the random walk spends a fraction of its time at a distance greater than $r$ from the origin can be expressed in terms of the probability that the walk spends a fraction of its time more than $s$ far from the origin, where $s$ is a value that depends on $r$ and the distribution of the walk's step lengths.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode.

In histopathology images, identifying and extracting nuclei is crucial for
automated analysis, yet it's a complex, time-consuming task even for medical
experts. To streamline this process, several methods have been proposed, but
they mostly focus on techniques like thresholding, segmentation, and clustering
without considering the underlying biology. Our goal was to create a more
biologically-informed approach, taking into account the distinctive features
and relationships of cancerous cells, to develop a method for detecting and
isolating nuclei in images. To this end, we propose a two-stage framework,
initially applying U-Net to generate a nucleus mask based on the input image,
then using a patch-based approach to refine the mask by leveraging local
histological information. To prepare and train the model, we developed a data
processing protocol that standardizes images and removes redundant patches,
also creating a publicly available dataset for training and evaluating the
model. In experiments, our model was applied to lung and colon cancer samples,
yielding the state-of-the-art results with Dice coefficients of 0.945 and 0.938
respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness and highlighting the importance of
integrating biological knowledge in the analysis.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F). The main goal of this research is to prove the converse theorem for the group G, which means if there is an irreducible automorphic representation of minimal non-trivial degree within the pair G x GLr+1, then it must correspond to a nontemporarily attached, automorphic representation of G.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory coupled with a scalar field can be expressed through the Chern-Simons form as $R_{ab}[e] = \kappa^2 T_{ab}$, where $T_{ab}$ represents a stress-energy tensor. Based on this formulation, we examine in detail the black hole and soliton configurations with spin and scalar fields, as well as the effects of external electromagnetic fields on them. We also discuss the possibility of reinterpreting this formulation as a correspondence between NTT gravity and a specific conformally invariant theory.

Elastography's effectiveness can be greatly enhanced by the estimation of both circumferential Young's modulus and lateral displacement, which are crucial for diagnosing various conditions. However, accurately determining lateral displacement near the probe is challenging due to corrupted data resulting from probe-induced motion and the limited sampling area available for synthetic aperture processing. To address this issue, a novel virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique is developed to enhance the estimation of both circumferential Young's modulus and lateral displacement near the probe. By recreating a larger sampling area through virtual sources in the beamforming process, VSSA significantly reduces probe-induced motion effects and provides a more precise estimate of lateral displacement. In vitro experiments using a phantom demonstrated that the developed VSSA technique could accurately determine both the circumferential Young's modulus and lateral displacement with mean errors of 0.35 kPa and 0.35 mm respectively. In addition, a comparison with a conventional SA and SA-SA techniques showed that VSSA and SA-SA techniques yield a 50 times and 10 times better correlation coefficient with the actual values respectively, while the developed VSSA technique yielded a 20% and 10% improvement in estimation accuracy over a large range of Young's modulus and displacement values respectively.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta d$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into distinct regions. This approach splits decision-making into two separate levels: a higher-level that selects a target region to move towards, and a lower-level for determining the specific actions to take within those regions. The lower-level decisions are made via isolated subproblems, while the higher-level considers the interconnected nature of the grid. A key aspect of this method involves using the outcomes of the subproblems to create an augmented state space, effectively making the higher-level level decisions independent of the original subproblems. However, unlike traditional methods, the discrete support of the actions in the augmented space remains tied to the local actions from the subproblems. We demonstrate the efficacy of this hierarchical model by incorporating various levels of cooperation at the boundary of regions, and show that it is capable of accurately 100% often reproducing existing data and also outperforms non-hierarchical methods by an average of 12% when evaluating it on a large randomly generated dataset of 100 different worlds.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we examine how a particular weak boson, specifically the $W$ boson, behaves when it interacts with itself and other particles, particularly Higgs bosons. A review of existing research is followed by a review of the principles of a General Gauge Boson Program, which includes the behavior of the $W$ boson in both its linear and nonlinear aspects. A comparison of the Effective Vector Boson Approximation and the General Gauge Boson Program in the linear and nonlinear regimes is presented, along with an examination of $WW$ scattering powered by a Higgs boson. A discussion on the parameters of the $W$ boson's effective theory, including how they are calculated and the impact of radiative effects, is also explored. A review of the programs that can calculate the parameters and calculate the impact of R\ega radiative effects on the $W$ boson's behavior is provided, along with an examination of the scattering off a $W$ boson in its linear aspect and the behavior of the $W$ boson in its nonlinear aspect in both the small and large momentum transfer regimes.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, which are filled with turbulent plasma that can cause pulsar signal scintillation, specifically metric scintillation, to occur. These screens can be localized to specific areas of the interstellar medium by identifying the positions of these scattering screens in relation to the line of sight to the pulsar. Pulsar B1133+16, which is a bright pulsar, has a direct line of sight to the Earth and its surrounding interstellar medium and has multiple scattering screens associated with it. These screens can be mapped to a small region of the interstellar medium surrounding it using scintillation data from various frequencies and polarizations and were found to have varying screen properties, including the distance from the Earth, the size of the screens, and the level of plasma density, which were determined by analyzing the wide-band scintillation patterns, scintillation dynamics, and the Doppler broadening of the pulsar's spectral components. To break through the one-second generation limit of text-to-speech systems
and create a system that can generate continuous, quasi-periodic audio in
real-time, a new architecture has been proposed for an autoregressive raw
waveform generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet. This system divides
the time domain into two segments: a fixed-length period for prediction and
an unlimited-length period for generation. Pitch-dependent dilated convolution
neural networks are applied within the prediction segment to provide the model
with information about time periods and intervals. A novel neural network
structure called Pitch-Adaptive Dilated Residual Neural Network was designed
and demonstrates significant improvements over existing systems through
generative duration and quality assessment methods. Quasi-Periodic WaveNet can
also be trained using a combination of multi-task learning and pitch
adapting, resulting in a system capable of generating high-quality audio at a
lower computational cost than WaveNet. Code for Quasi-Periodic WaveNet has
been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenwen0818/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties analogous to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. To achieve this, we develop a two-phase approach for modeling both easy and challenging cases. In the first phase, we use a simple, transfer learning-based method to easily model instances with clear visual references, such as speech produced by talking heads. In the second phase, we employ an adversarial latent variable model to difficult cases with no obvious visual cues. We evaluate both easy and challenging cases and present ablation studies to demonstrate the benefits of our approach. Our algorithm ranks second in the audio-visual localisation challenge without access to training labels.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs, which are more accurately represented using non-Euclidean geometry, specifically Lorentzian space. A major limitation of existing GCN methods is their failure to account for the true distances between nodes, leading to suboptimal results. In an attempt to rectify this issue, we introduced the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which leverages Lorentzian geometry to redefine the convolution operation and calculate the distance between nodes more accurately. By controlling hyperparameter configurations, we found that LGCN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art GCN methods on multiple datasets, including Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed, by a margin of 15% to 20%. Moreover, our results showed that the Lorentzian GCN excels in particular in modeling robust hierarchical structures, as evident from its superior performance on hierarchical graph generation tasks.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model in its basic and
risk-sensitive forms, where the model parameter kappa controls the degree of
nonlinearity, with potential applications to explain anomalous discounting
behavior observed in psychology and neuroscience. As a starting point, we start
with the Tsallis delay discounting model proposed by Takahashi in 2014 and
transform it into the exponential form by applying a specific transformation
to its utility function. We then derive the risk-sensitive and quadratic versions
of the model for comparison purposes. We also discuss the relationship between
our model and other delay discounting models, including the hyperbolic and
quadratic models. Furthermore, we validate our model using empirical data from
psychology and neuroscience studies, and analyze its fitted parameters to
draw inferences about the underlying neural mechanisms associated with it. We
further explore the possibility of approximating our model as a specific form of
the risk-sensitive and quadratic models, and analyze its implications for the
prediction of decision-making related phenomena such as cocaine use disorder.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the dark sector parameters and neutrino masses, determining the parameter ranges that meet both experimental requirements, including dark matter abundance and neutrino mass constraints, as well as the Higgs field's stability in the presence of quantum fluctuations. By conducting a parameter scan and employing the renormalization group, we determine the relationship between the running and effective couplings, which influence Higgs vacuum stability, neutrino masses, and dark matter behavior. Consequently, we identify the minimum quark masses and coupling constants that ensure both Higgs vacuum stability and neutrino mass compliance across a broad energy spectrum.

We investigated the mixing of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbitals in 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal oxides using a combination of experimental and theoretical techniques.
Core-level spectroscopy was used to analyze the local electronic states and determine the degree of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in various compounds with different crystal field splitting energies ($\Delta$).
A theoretical framework was developed to calculate the spin and orbital moments in transition metal oxides with correlated $d$ electrons, and it was applied to a wide range of compounds spanning different $\Delta$ values and oxidation states.
The results showed that in compounds with $\Delta$ greater than 1 eV, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing is minimal and can be neglected, whereas in compounds with $\Delta$ less than 1 eV, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing becomes significant and cannot be ignored.
Consequently, the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing must be taken into account when interpreting experimental data and it also has important implications for the theoretical modeling of transition metal oxides with $\Delta$ less than 1 eV.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology behaves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays and reconstructs specific pathologies visible on radiologist notes. By reconfiguring the generated images, we successfully discovered a way to edit X-rays based on radiologist notes for better machine learning model training. Moreover, our research included an unusual approach to define a normal class for dataset separation as well as an uncommon evaluation of the CycleGAN's accuracy in editing X-rays, utilizing the CheXpert dataset and radiologist notes. The results and methodology have been presented in a data-driven and quantitative manner. In the hope of advancing disease-aware image editing and providing a foundation for the usage of GAN in medical imaging, our research has been made available on GitHub for public use.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
